slides.title: Fair questions first
slides.text: A survey asks people questions. The answers can only be fair if the questions are fair.
slides.alt: My Data in Pro: a survey question and its answer rows, where fairness starts with how the question is asked.

slides.title: Leading questions
slides.text: A question that pushes people toward one answer is a leading question. It builds bias into the data before anyone counts.
slides.alt: A second Pro survey question: its wording matters, because a pushing question bends the data before counting.

slides.title: Fix the question
slides.text: Ask in a way that lets every answer feel equally welcome.
steps: leading: Don't you agree homework is too long?
fair: Is homework too long, about right or too short?
slides.alt: One Grade Asked: a fairness case about who a survey asked, and who it never reached.

slides.title: A bigger, fairer sample
slides.text: More answers from more kinds of people make a fairer sample. Even a few missing answers can change a close result.
slides.alt: Who Is Missing? The fairness case that asks which people a sample left out before trusting its answer.

slides.title: Compare by percent
slides.text: Your class: 18 of 25 walk to school. Another class: 20 of 40. Compare 72% with 50%, not 18 with 20.
slides.alt: A third survey question in My Data: the case for comparing classes by percent instead of raw counts.

slides.title: Dot's piece lights up
slides.text: Dot's piece clicks into place — two of four, and the Spark is shining. Next, Pim the owl is waiting at the post office, with a town full of letters to deliver.

slides.title: Your mission
slides.text: Open Data Detective at My Data. Chart one survey question, clean it, and compare it with another class by percent.
